meta.source: Authored from PSLE composition research + english/knowledge-base/*
meta.note: Essay elevation handles for Continuous Writing (36 marks: Content 18 + Language 18). Band descriptors referenced here are a reconstruction triangulated from Singapore tuition-centre guidance; SEAB does not publish composition rubrics.
deploymentRules: Two to four idioms maximum in a 300-450 word composition. Zero is safer than three forced ones.
Never place an idiom in the opening sentence or in the climax paragraph. Dialogue is the safest home for an idiom.
Three to four well-placed sensory details across the whole composition, densest at the point of highest tension.
Maximum two similes, and neither may be a memorised one.
One strong verb beats a weak verb plus two adverbs.
Show the value through what the character does. Never announce it in the last line.

idioms.meaning: to force yourself to do something unpleasant that you have been putting off
idioms.useWhen: the moment the character stops avoiding and finally acts, usually at the start of the climax or just before an apology
idioms.example: I bit the bullet, walked to the staffroom door and knocked before I could change my mind.
idioms.note: Works best when the unpleasant thing is named in the same sentence, so the idiom carries the action rather than decorating it.

idioms.meaning: to keep going through pain or difficulty without complaining
idioms.useWhen: mid-effort in a sports, exam or caregiving story, when the character is losing but continues
idioms.example: My calves were burning by the third lap, so I gritted my teeth and kept my eyes on Wei Ming's heels.
idioms.note: Pair it with one physical detail; on its own it can read as filler.

idioms.useWhen: the falling action, summarising a long stretch of hardship in one clause
idioms.example: We weathered the storm together that year, sharing one fan and two study tables in the same bedroom.
idioms.note: Strong for family hardship stories. Avoid if your story already has literal rain in it.

idioms.meaning: a struggle that stays difficult the whole way
idioms.useWhen: the build-up, when the reader needs to know the problem will not be solved quickly
idioms.example: Teaching my grandmother to use the new bus app was an uphill battle, and we were only on step two after forty minutes.
idioms.note: Follow it immediately with the concrete detail that proves the difficulty.

idioms.useWhen: just after the character learns how big the problem is
idioms.example: Two hundred flyers, one afternoon and eleven blocks: we had a mountain to climb.
idioms.note: Best when you supply the numbers, so the mountain has a size.

idioms.meaning: despite everything being unlikely to work
idioms.useWhen: the resolution of an underdog story
idioms.example: Against all odds, the little cactus my brother had almost thrown away pushed out a flower in June.
idioms.note: Only earns its place if the odds were shown earlier. Otherwise it is a claim with no evidence.

idioms.meaning: to perform well when it matters most
idioms.useWhen: the climax resolution, when a quiet character surprises everyone
idioms.example: Siti had never spoken in assembly before, but she rose to the occasion and read all four paragraphs without once looking down.
idioms.note: Give the reader the proof in the same sentence, as in the example.

idioms.meaning: to refuse to give in under pressure
idioms.useWhen: a peer-pressure or bullying story, at the point of refusal
idioms.example: Three of them were waiting for me to laugh along, and for the first time in my life I stood my ground and said nothing.
idioms.note: Excellent for integrity stories because it shows a choice rather than a feeling.

idioms.meaning: to stay calm when you are frightened
idioms.useWhen: the seconds before a performance, a race or a confession
idioms.example: The recorder was slippery in my hands, but I held my nerve and waited for Mrs Lim's count of four.

idioms.useWhen: the build-up of a story about being overloaded
idioms.example: Between two CCAs and my sister's fever, I was just keeping my head above water that week.
idioms.note: Do not use in a story that also involves swimming or a flood; the literal clash reads as clumsy.

idioms.meaning: to become comfortable in a new situation
idioms.useWhen: the transition after a move, a new school or a new team
idioms.example: It took me a whole term to find my feet at Bukit View, and the first friend I made was the one who lent me a compass.
idioms.note: Good for new-school topics, which are extremely common PSLE prompts.

idioms.meaning: to learn how something is done
idioms.useWhen: a job-shadowing, helping-at-the-stall or new-CCA story
idioms.example: By the third Saturday at my uncle's drinks stall I had learnt the ropes: ice first, syrup second, never the other way round.

idioms.meaning: to succeed or fail with no help available
idioms.useWhen: the moment the character is left alone with the problem
idioms.example: Mr Rahman handed me the microphone and stepped back. It was sink or swim.
idioms.note: Very effective as a short sentence on its own line before the climax.

idioms.phrase: at the end of my tether
idioms.meaning: to have no patience or energy left
idioms.useWhen: the lowest point, just before the character either gives up or changes
idioms.example: After the fourth phone call went unanswered I was at the end of my tether, sitting on the void deck bench with the bag of medicine on my lap.
idioms.note: This is the low point marker. Do not use it twice.

idioms.meaning: the final small thing that makes a situation unbearable
idioms.useWhen: the trigger event that starts the climax
idioms.example: When he knocked my project into the drain and laughed, that was the last straw.

idioms.meaning: to take the worst part of something
idioms.useWhen: showing that one character suffered more than the others
idioms.example: My mother bore the brunt of it, cycling to the market at six so we could still have breakfast.

idioms.useWhen: as the temptation the character rejects, not the choice they take
idioms.example: Every part of me wanted to throw in the towel, so I put my shoes on before that part could finish its sentence.
idioms.note: Strongest when refused. If your character actually gives up, use it plainly and pay the consequence.

idioms.useWhen: the beginning of the recovery paragraph
idioms.example: I picked myself up, wiped the gravel out of my knee with my sleeve and asked the coach for one more go.

idioms.meaning: to finish something you started, despite difficulty
idioms.useWhen: the decision that ends the story
idioms.example: Nobody would have blamed me for stopping at block 12, but I had promised eleven letters and I meant to see it through.

idioms.meaning: to refuse to change your mind
idioms.useWhen: a stubbornness that the character later regrets, or a principled refusal
idioms.example: I dug my heels in and refused to apologise, and the seat beside me stayed empty for a week.

idioms.useWhen: the seconds before something is revealed
idioms.example: With my heart in my mouth, I lifted the lid of the shoebox where the hamster should have been.

idioms.useWhen: the falling action, right after the danger passes
idioms.example: The lorry passed close enough to move my hair. It was a close shave, and my legs only started shaking afterwards.

idioms.phrase: break out in a cold sweat
idioms.useWhen: the instant the character realises something has gone wrong
idioms.example: I broke out in a cold sweat when I patted my pocket and found no EZ-link card in it.

idioms.meaning: unable to move from fear or shock
idioms.useWhen: the freeze moment at the top of the climax
idioms.example: The dog stopped growling and looked straight at me, and I stood rooted to the spot beside the bicycle rack.

idioms.useWhen: at a discovery, never at a mild surprise
idioms.example: My blood ran cold when I heard my own name coming from inside the principal's office.

idioms.phrase: out of the frying pan into the fire
idioms.meaning: to escape one problem and land in a worse one
idioms.useWhen: a second complication immediately after the first is solved
idioms.example: I had finally found the missing file, and then I saw the date on it: out of the frying pan into the fire.

idioms.meaning: in a risky position where one mistake will cause trouble
idioms.useWhen: when a character has already been warned once
idioms.example: After the second late slip I knew I was on thin ice with Mrs Chua.

idioms.useWhen: immediately before impact, news or confrontation
idioms.example: I braced myself, pushed the gate open and counted the steps to the front door.

idioms.meaning: to wait tensely for an outcome
idioms.useWhen: the pause inside the climax
idioms.example: The whole class held its breath while the results slid out of the printer one line at a time.

idioms.phrase: the hair on my neck stood up
idioms.meaning: to feel a sudden instinctive fear
idioms.useWhen: an atmosphere moment in a night or empty-building scene
idioms.example: The lift doors closed on an empty lobby and the hair on my neck stood up.

idioms.meaning: to admit the truth after hiding it
idioms.useWhen: the confession that resolves an integrity story
idioms.example: I came clean about the broken window, standing in the corridor with the cricket ball still in my hand.

idioms.useWhen: in dialogue, where it sounds most natural
idioms.example: "Somebody has to own up," Mr Tan said, and the classroom got so quiet I could hear the fan.

idioms.meaning: to accept the punishment for what you did
idioms.useWhen: the walk towards the consequence
idioms.example: There was no point stretching it out any longer, so I went to face the music at the general office.

idioms.meaning: to admit you were wrong after boasting
idioms.useWhen: after a character's pride is punctured
idioms.example: I had told everyone I would win the semi-final easily, and now I had to eat humble pie in front of the whole team.

idioms.meaning: to accept embarrassment in order to do the right thing
idioms.useWhen: just before asking for help or apologising
idioms.example: I swallowed my pride and asked Devi, the girl I had ignored all term, whether she could explain question nine.

idioms.meaning: to do something to correct a wrong
idioms.useWhen: the resolution, expressed as an action rather than an apology
idioms.example: To make amends I spent both recesses that week helping her rebuild the model with new lolly sticks.

idioms.meaning: to change your behaviour for the better
idioms.useWhen: sparingly, and only if the new behaviour is shown
idioms.example: I turned over a new leaf that term, which in practice meant packing my bag the night before instead of at 6.40 a.m.
idioms.note: Common but still usable, provided you immediately give the small concrete proof, as in the example. Without proof it reads as a memorised phrase.

idioms.meaning: relief after a burden is removed
idioms.useWhen: immediately after a confession or a difficult conversation
idioms.example: Telling my father was like taking a weight off my shoulders, and I ate dinner properly for the first time in three days.

idioms.meaning: the feeling of having done nothing wrong
idioms.useWhen: the final reflection of an honesty story
idioms.example: I lost the prize, but I slept that night with a clear conscience.

idioms.meaning: caught in the act of doing something wrong
idioms.useWhen: the exposure moment
idioms.example: He was caught red-handed with three packets of sweets and no receipt.

idioms.meaning: to go further than what is acceptable
idioms.useWhen: the moment a joke turns cruel
idioms.example: The teasing had been ordinary until he mentioned her father, and then he crossed the line.

idioms.useWhen: the accidental betrayal of a secret
idioms.example: It was a slip of the tongue, six words long, and it cost me my best friend.

idioms.useWhen: the confession scene in a blame story
idioms.example: I stood up at the end of the period and set the record straight: Aiman had not touched the projector.

idioms.meaning: to accept criticism or defeat without complaining
idioms.useWhen: the ending of a story where the character loses and grows
idioms.example: I took it on the chin, shook the other captain's hand and asked him where he had learnt that serve.

idioms.meaning: someone who listens when you are upset
idioms.useWhen: the friendship resolution
idioms.example: She did not need advice that afternoon; she needed a shoulder to cry on and a seat in the shade.

idioms.meaning: to make a special effort for someone
idioms.useWhen: showing kindness through inconvenience
idioms.example: He went out of his way to walk me to the bus stop, even though his block was in the opposite direction.

idioms.useWhen: in dialogue or in a quick action beat
idioms.example: "Lend a hand with the tables," my form teacher said, and eleven of us stayed back until the hall was empty.

idioms.useWhen: describing a grandparent, cleaner or neighbour who is rough on the outside
idioms.example: Uncle Rahim shouted at everyone about their shoes and had a heart of gold underneath it.

idioms.useWhen: the realisation just before the character changes
idioms.example: Only when I put myself in her shoes did I understand why she never joined us at the canteen.

idioms.phrase: give him the benefit of the doubt
idioms.meaning: to choose to believe someone despite suspicion
idioms.useWhen: a misunderstanding story, at the turning point
idioms.example: I decided to give him the benefit of the doubt and asked him what had really happened before I told anyone else.

idioms.useWhen: the reconciliation, best in narration not dialogue
idioms.example: We buried the hatchet over two bowls of fishball noodles that neither of us finished.

idioms.useWhen: when the character makes the first move after a fight
idioms.example: I held out an olive branch in the form of a badly wrapped birthday present left on her desk.

idioms.useWhen: the moment of courage in a bullying story
idioms.example: Nobody stuck up for her, so I put my tray down and said her name out loud.

idioms.useWhen: usually in the negative, to establish a conflict
idioms.example: My brother and I had not seen eye to eye about the fan setting since the day he moved into my room.

idioms.useWhen: the reflection of a friendship story
idioms.example: Through thick and thin, and two whole years of different classes, she still saved me the seat by the window.

idioms.meaning: to remove tension by talking honestly
idioms.useWhen: the conversation that resolves the conflict
idioms.example: We cleared the air on the walk home, which took twice as long as usual.

idioms.useWhen: the falling action
idioms.example: It took a whole weekend and one shared umbrella to patch things up.

idioms.useWhen: an introduction scene
idioms.example: We hit it off in the queue for the water cooler, arguing about which primary school had the better field.

idioms.useWhen: the resolution of a sibling or team argument
idioms.example: We met halfway: he got the fan, I got the desk lamp, and neither of us was fully satisfied.

idioms.useWhen: the build-up, to name a long-running conflict quickly
idioms.example: My father and my uncle had been at loggerheads about the shop since before I was born.

idioms.meaning: to make a tense first meeting easier
idioms.useWhen: the first exchange between strangers
idioms.example: I broke the ice by asking him whether the vending machine had eaten his coins too.

idioms.useWhen: when a third character intervenes
idioms.example: Our class monitor smoothed things over before Mrs Goh came back from the photocopy room.

idioms.meaning: to work late into the night
idioms.useWhen: the preparation montage of an effort story
idioms.example: I burnt the midnight oil for a week, and my mother found me asleep on the science file twice.
idioms.note: Frequently used but still accurate. Add the specific detail of what you were doing so it is not a stock phrase.

idioms.meaning: to do your fair share of work
idioms.useWhen: a group-project story
idioms.example: For the first two weeks I did not pull my weight, and the slides showed it.

idioms.meaning: to search or try everything possible
idioms.useWhen: a searching scene
idioms.example: We left no stone unturned looking for the key, including the drain grating and the shoe rack of every neighbour on the floor.

idioms.meaning: to accept a duty nobody assigned you
idioms.useWhen: the moment the character chooses responsibility
idioms.example: I took it upon myself to water the class plants during the holidays, and told nobody I was doing it.

idioms.useWhen: the ending of a responsibility story
idioms.example: I had promised to be there at seven, so I stood by my word and waited under the block until he came down at ten past.

idioms.phrase: keep my end of the bargain
idioms.meaning: to do the part you agreed to do
idioms.useWhen: a deal made earlier in the story
idioms.example: He had kept his end of the bargain, so I sat down and did the washing up without being asked twice.

idioms.useWhen: the unexpected event that starts the plot
idioms.example: Out of the blue, a girl I had never spoken to asked whether I wanted her spare recorder.

idioms.useWhen: the news that changes everything, used once only
idioms.example: The news that the stall was closing came like a bolt from the blue on an ordinary Tuesday.

idioms.useWhen: the falling action
idioms.example: Finding the wallet under the bench was a load off my mind, though my hands took a while to agree.

idioms.meaning: to surprise someone who is unprepared
idioms.useWhen: an unexpected kindness or an unexpected question
idioms.example: His apology caught me off guard, because I had spent the whole morning preparing to be angry.

idioms.useWhen: the realisation, in the falling action
idioms.example: It dawned on me, somewhere between the third and fourth floor, that she had been waiting for me to ask.

idioms.useWhen: the realisation, expressed compactly
idioms.example: Then the penny dropped: the handwriting on the card was my grandmother's.

idioms.useWhen: the flashpoint of an anger story
idioms.example: When he called her that name for the second time, I saw red and pushed his chair.

idioms.useWhen: showing a character's flaw
idioms.example: My father almost never flew off the handle, which was why the silence at dinner frightened me more than shouting would have.

idioms.useWhen: a mistake the character regrets
idioms.example: I lost my cool in front of the whole canteen and regretted it before I had finished the sentence.

idioms.meaning: to stop yourself from saying something
idioms.useWhen: the restraint that shows growth
idioms.example: I bit my tongue, counted to five and let her finish.

idioms.useWhen: the hesitation before the climax
idioms.example: Halfway up the stairs I had second thoughts and sat down on the landing with the letter in my hand.

idioms.meaning: to be annoyed at your own mistake
idioms.useWhen: regret, in the falling action
idioms.example: I could have kicked myself: the answer had been in the second paragraph the whole time.

idioms.phrase: wish the ground would swallow me up
idioms.useWhen: a public humiliation scene
idioms.example: My name came out of the loudspeaker with the wrong pronunciation for the third year running, and I wished the ground would swallow me up.

idioms.meaning: to admit you were wrong about something you said confidently
idioms.useWhen: after a boast is disproved
idioms.example: I had to eat my words when the quietest boy in the class scored full marks.

idioms.useWhen: in a short action beat rather than as a stated emotion
idioms.example: I hung my head and studied the grout between two floor tiles.

idioms.meaning: the feeling of being close to tears
idioms.useWhen: farewell or gratitude scenes
idioms.example: There was a lump in my throat when she pressed the packet of biscuits into my hand at the lift lobby.
idioms.note: Frequent but physically accurate. Use once, and never in the same paragraph as any other body-part phrase.

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: It was raining cats and dogs when I left the school gate.
idioms.note: The single most-flagged dead idiom in Singapore marking commentary. Instead write what the rain did: 'The rain came down hard enough to bounce off the covered walkway.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: My little sister was the apple of my eye.
idioms.note: The standard example of an idiom bolted into the wrong story. Instead show the treasuring: 'I gave her the last chicken wing without being asked, which I had never once done for anyone else.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: I crept in as quiet as a mouse.
idioms.note: Dead simile; no image survives. Instead: 'I put my weight on the outside of each foot, the way I had learnt on the noisy third step.'

idioms.meaning: just before it was too late
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: The teacher arrived in the nick of time.
idioms.note: Signals a convenient rescue, which costs Content marks. Instead let your character solve the problem, and give the exact time: 'The bell went eleven seconds after I sat down.'

idioms.meaning: something bad that turns out well
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: Losing the match was a blessing in disguise.
idioms.note: States the moral for the reader. Instead show the benefit: 'Losing meant an extra term of Tuesday trainings, which was how I met Haziq.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: Time flies, and soon it was the last day of term.
idioms.note: Filler transition. Instead mark time with a detail: 'By the time the flame-of-the-forest outside our block had dropped all its flowers, we were friends.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: We went to the beach once in a blue moon.
idioms.note: Rarely fits a one-day narrative. Instead give the actual frequency: 'We had been to the beach twice, both times for a cousin's birthday.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: The test was a piece of cake.
idioms.note: Undercuts the conflict you have just built. Instead show the ease: 'I finished section A with eleven minutes to spare and checked it twice out of suspicion.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: I was over the moon when I saw my result.
idioms.note: Joy told, not shown. Instead: 'I read the slip three times, then read it again in case it changed.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: I was on cloud nine for the rest of the day.
idioms.note: Same problem as 'over the moon'. Instead show one behaviour the joy caused: 'I walked past my bus stop and only noticed at the next block.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: I had butterflies in my stomach before my turn.
idioms.note: The most saturated nervousness phrase in P5 and P6 scripts. Instead: 'I had eaten nothing since breakfast and still did not feel hungry.'

idioms.phrase: beads of perspiration trickled down my forehead
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: Beads of perspiration trickled down my forehead as I waited.
idioms.note: The definitive Singapore composition cliche; markers can recite it. Instead: 'My palm left a damp mark on the paper, so I moved my hand to the desk.'

idioms.phrase: my heart pounded like a drum
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: My heart pounded like a drum as I opened the door.
idioms.note: The simile is inert. Instead: 'Something in my chest was hitting the inside of my ribs, asking to be let out.'

idioms.phrase: as fast as my legs could carry me
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: I ran home as fast as my legs could carry me.
idioms.note: Instead use one strong verb plus a landmark: 'I tore past the bicycle bays and did not slow down until the lift lobby.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: He ran like the wind towards the finish line.
idioms.note: Instead: 'He was three strides ahead by the bend and stretching it.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: She turned as white as a sheet.
idioms.note: Instead show the shock elsewhere: 'She sat down on the step without checking whether it was clean.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: I was sweating like a pig by the second lap.
idioms.note: Register is too low for PSLE writing. Instead: 'My shirt had gone dark down the middle of my back.'

idioms.phrase: at the top of my lungs
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: I shouted at the top of my lungs.
idioms.note: Instead choose a loud speech verb and give the effect: 'I bellowed his name, and two aunties at the drying rack turned round.'

idioms.phrase: tears streamed down my cheeks like a waterfall
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: Tears streamed down my cheeks like a waterfall.
idioms.note: Over-simile. Instead: 'I turned the tap on so nobody would hear.'

idioms.phrase: I heaved a sigh of relief
idioms.useWhen: at most once, and only if nothing else in the paragraph is a stock phrase
idioms.example: I heaved a sigh of relief when the lights came back on.
idioms.note: Acceptable once, dead as a habit, and most students use it three times. Instead: 'My shoulders came down from somewhere near my ears.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: Little did I know that the day would end differently.
idioms.note: Telegraphs the twist so the marker predicts your story. Instead end the paragraph on the ordinary detail and let the surprise arrive unannounced.

idioms.phrase: kill two birds with one stone
idioms.meaning: to achieve two things with one action
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: I killed two birds with one stone by going to the library after tuition.
idioms.note: Rarely fits a narrative and sounds adult. Instead simply narrate both outcomes.

idioms.phrase: don't judge a book by its cover
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: I learnt that you should not judge a book by its cover.
idioms.note: A proverb doing the reflection's job badly. Instead show the corrected judgement: 'I had thought he was showing off. He had been practising for his sister.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: That day I learnt that honesty is the best policy.
idioms.note: Announces the value. Instead: 'I did not feel brave. I only felt lighter.'

idioms.meaning: what you do matters more than what you say
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: Actions speak louder than words, I realised.
idioms.note: Instead close on the action itself and let it speak: 'On Monday I arrived ten minutes early and stacked the chairs before anyone asked.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: Practice makes perfect, and I finally got it right.
idioms.note: Instead give the count: 'The forty-first attempt was the one that held.'

idioms.phrase: every cloud has a silver lining
idioms.meaning: bad situations have a good side
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: Every cloud has a silver lining, after all.
idioms.note: Instead name the specific good thing that came out of the bad one.

idioms.meaning: late is better than not at all
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: Better late than never, I suppose.
idioms.note: Weak closing move. Instead: 'I was four days late with the apology. She took it anyway.'

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: My cousin was the black sheep of the family.
idioms.note: Labels a character instead of showing them. Instead give one behaviour the family disapproves of.

idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: He said he would apologise when pigs fly.
idioms.note: Register mismatch for PSLE narrative. Instead use plain refusal in dialogue.

idioms.phrase: give someone a piece of my mind
idioms.meaning: to tell someone angrily what you think
idioms.useWhen: usable, but the anger must be shown too
idioms.example: I marched over to give him a piece of my mind and forgot every word of it once I got there.
idioms.note: Survives if the outcome is unexpected, as in the example. On its own it is a stock phrase.

idioms.phrase: no use crying over spilt milk
idioms.meaning: no point regretting what cannot be changed
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: There was no use crying over spilt milk.
idioms.note: Proverb-as-moral. Instead show the character choosing the next action: 'The vase was in four pieces. I fetched the dustpan.'

idioms.phrase: a friend in need is a friend indeed
idioms.useWhen: do not use
idioms.example: A friend in need is a friend indeed.
idioms.note: Instead close on what the friend actually did, with no comment attached.

valuesVocab.whenToUse: Stories where the character fails first and continues anyway: a lost match, a failed audition, a subject that will not improve, an injury, a family setback. Resilience is recovery after failure, so your plot must contain a genuine failure, not just a difficulty.
phrases: steeled myself for the second attempt
refused to be beaten by a hill I had already climbed twice
dug deeper than I knew I could
my legs disagreed; I went anyway
the third attempt was the one that held
I had failed twice and I would not fail quietly
set my jaw and started again
quitting was available and I did not take it
the finish line had not moved, only my excuses had
I stopped counting the failures and started counting the attempts
reflectionLines: I am not faster than I was in March. I am only harder to stop.
The wall was still there. I had simply learnt where to put my hands.
I did not beat him. I finished, which last year I did not.

valuesVocab.whenToUse: Stories where the character is trusted with something and nobody is watching: a younger sibling, the class keys, a group project, a neighbour's cat, money for the market. The test of responsibility is the moment supervision disappears.
phrases: the job was mine to finish
nobody was watching, which was exactly the point
I had given my word in front of four people
I took it upon myself
shouldered the blame without shifting any of it
I stayed until the last chair was stacked
the consequence had my name on it
I checked twice because once was how mistakes happened
I did the boring half as well
reflectionLines: Being trusted is not a compliment. It is a bill that arrives later.
I did not want the task. I wanted to be the kind of person who finishes one.
Nobody thanked me for the second hour. That was the hour that counted.

valuesVocab.whenToUse: Stories involving elders, cleaners, security guards, teachers, or a classmate the narrator has been dismissing. Respect stories work best when the narrator starts out unknowingly disrespectful, so the change is visible.
phrases: I let her finish
I lowered my voice before I lowered my opinion
I had spoken over her for two years without noticing
he had earned the right to be heard
treated the cleaner the way I treated the principal
I returned the greeting properly this time
I used his name instead of pointing
I stood up before she had to ask
reflectionLines: Respect is not what you say to someone. It is what you stop doing.
He had been sweeping our corridor for six years. I had known his name for one day.
I had been polite. Polite and respectful, it turns out, are not the same thing.

valuesVocab.whenToUse: Stories where the wrong thing is easy and undetectable: found money, an open answer key, a mistake nobody saw, a friend who cheated. Integrity requires the character to have a genuine chance of getting away with it.
phrases: the answer key was open on the desk and I closed it
nobody would ever have known, which was the whole problem
my conscience kept better records than my teacher did
I handed it back before I could talk myself out of it
the lie was small, which was what made it easy and what made it wrong
I told the truth badly, but I told it
the fifty dollars stayed in my pocket and got heavier every hour
reflectionLines: Integrity is what is left when the risk of being caught is removed.
I did not feel brave. I only felt lighter.
I lost the prize. I got to keep the version of myself I had been pretending to be.

valuesVocab.whenToUse: Stories about noticing: a classmate eating alone, a grandparent who has gone quiet, a neighbour struggling with groceries, an injured animal. The AL1 move is that the character notices before being asked.
phrases: I noticed before I was asked
I sat with him and said nothing useful for ten minutes
she needed company, not advice
I gave up my seat and my excuse at the same time
kindness cost me a bus ride and bought me a friend
I put myself in her shoes and found that they pinched
I saved her the seat without mentioning it
reflectionLines: Kindness is mostly noticing. The doing is the easy half.
She never said thank you. She simply sat down, which was the same thing.
It cost me twenty minutes. I had been prepared to spend them on nothing at all.

valuesVocab.whenToUse: Stories about difference and repair: a quarrel with a sibling, a class split into camps, neighbours of different backgrounds, a festival shared across families. Harmony is not agreement; it is people choosing to live well together despite disagreement.
phrases: we met halfway and both of us limped there
different names for the same festival, the same food on both tables
the argument had two sides and I had only listened to mine
we were louder together than either of us had been apart
I stopped keeping score
our doors faced each other for nine years before I knocked on his
reflectionLines: We did not agree. We simply stopped needing to.
The corridor between our flats is four steps long. It took me nine years to walk it.
We are not the same. We are, it turns out, on the same side.

valuesVocab.whenToUse: Stories where a quiet sacrifice is discovered late: a parent's second job, a teacher who stayed back, a grandparent's daily routine. The plot must contain the discovery, otherwise gratitude is only a statement.
phrases: I had thanked her a hundred times and meant it once
the receipt in her purse was dated three months before mine
she had been getting up at five for eleven years and had never mentioned it
I had eaten that breakfast every day without once asking who made it
I said thank you properly, using her name
reflectionLines: I had said thank you every morning for six years. On Tuesday I finally meant it.
The bus fare was one dollar and forty cents. She had paid it four hundred times.
I did not tell her I knew. I simply started washing up.

valuesVocab.whenToUse: Stories where the frightening thing is small and social: speaking up, going first, admitting ignorance, defending someone unpopular. Physical danger is the weaker choice because it happens to the character rather than being chosen.
phrases: I put my hand up before my brain could object
I went first, which was the only difficult part
my voice came out smaller than I planned and I kept going
I said her name out loud in a room that had decided not to
courage was thirty seconds long and then it was over
reflectionLines: I was not brave. I was just first.
Courage, it turns out, is mostly a matter of who moves first.
My hand was still shaking when I sat down. It had gone up anyway.

valuesVocab.whenToUse: Stories built on a misjudgement: the classmate you thought was rude, the sibling you thought was lazy, the parent you thought did not care. The turning point is information the narrator did not have.
phrases: I had built a whole opinion out of one afternoon
her rudeness had a reason and the reason was at home
I had been reading his silence wrongly for a year
the story I had told myself about him had one character in it and it was me
I asked instead of assuming
reflectionLines: I had known him for two years and met him on Thursday.
He was not being difficult. He was being tired, and I had never asked.
I changed my mind about her, which cost nothing and took two years.

valuesVocab.whenToUse: Stories where the narrator is good at something and is beaten, corrected, or out-taught by someone they underestimated. Humility needs an earlier moment of pride for the fall to matter.
phrases: I had come to teach him and he taught me the grip
the boy I had ignored knew the answer to question nine
I asked for help out loud, in front of people
I had been the best in a very small room
I gave the credit to the person who had actually done the work
reflectionLines: I had come to teach him. He taught me the grip.
I was the best in my class. My class had thirty-nine people in it and the world does not.
Asking took four seconds. Pretending had taken me a term.

weakToStrong.note: Tired or unwilling: trudged, plodded, shuffled. Confident: strode, marched. Quiet: crept, padded. Unsteady: staggered, lurched. Pick for the mood, not for the length of the word.
Bolted and fled carry fear. Sprinted and raced carry effort. Darted is short and repeatable; hurtled is out of control.
Keep plain 'said' for most of the dialogue so the loaded verbs land. One strong tag every four or five lines is plenty.
Glanced is brief, studied is long, peered means the view is difficult, scanned means you are searching.
'Went' hides both the manner and the mood. Replacing it usually adds a free piece of characterisation.
Snatched and seized are fast and rude. Clutched is fearful. Plucked is delicate.
The care in the verb tells the reader the character's state: 'eased the cup down' versus 'dropped the cup'.
'Got' is the single most common weak verb in P6 scripts. Any replacement is an improvement.
If 'made' means 'forced someone to', use forced, pressed or persuaded.
'Made out' is excellent in low light: 'I could just make out the number on the gate.'
'Picked at' shows worry without naming it. This is a free show-don't-tell move.
'Laughed one second later than everyone else' shows guilt or exclusion better than any single verb.
'Blinked hard' is stronger than 'cried' because it shows resistance, which is more interesting than tears.
Cradled is gentle, clutched is desperate, pinned is forceful.
Tossed is casual, hurled is angry, lobbed is high and gentle.
Nudged and eased are polite; shoved and barged are not. This verb often defines your antagonist.
For accidents use clipped or caught: 'the door caught my elbow'.
Crumpled and slumped suggest the body giving up; toppled and tumbled are mechanical.
'Perched on the edge of the chair' shows nervousness in three words.
Hovered is uncertain, planted myself is defiant, loomed is threatening.
If the jump is from surprise, use flinched or started, not jumped.
Inched and edged buy tension for free because they slow the reader down.
Better still, replace the adjective with a measurement: 'the queue reached the second pillar'.
Cramped and narrow describe the effect on people, which is more useful than size alone.
'Nice' tells the marker nothing. Choose the exact quality you mean, then prove it with one action.
Name the specific fault. 'Bad' is a placeholder you left in by accident.
For work use accurate or careful; for people use reliable or decent.
Better still, do not name it. Show one behaviour the happiness caused.
Crestfallen is precise: it means hope has just been removed.
'Cold' is the strongest of these in a P6 story, because quiet anger is rarer on the page.
Warning: swapping 'scared' for 'petrified' is still telling. Use the body instead.
Or show it: 'I took the stairs one at a time, both feet on each step'.
Match the word to what is hard: a task is demanding, a person is stubborn, weather is unforgiving.

strong: <delete it and upgrade the next word>
weakToStrong.note: 'Very tired' becomes 'exhausted'. 'Very big' becomes 'enormous'. Every 'very' in your script is one unused stronger word.
Numbers are more vivid than quantities. Specific beats large.
Never leave 'thing' in a final draft. Name it: the ruler, the letter, the blue file, the packet of biscuits.
'Stuff' is spoken English. In Continuous Writing it costs Language marks.
Shrill and piercing are high; booming and thunderous are low. They are not interchangeable.
'Still' describes the room; 'hushed' describes the people in it.
Stifling and airless describe indoor Singapore heat better than 'hot' ever will.
For an air-conditioned hall, 'the cold had a metal taste to it' beats any single adjective.
Use 'elderly' for people and 'weathered' or 'battered' for objects. Never swap them.
Best replaced entirely: 'I had packed the bag twice and unpacked it once, just to pack it again'.

openers.template: [Character] was already [doing the urgent thing] when [the complication arrived].
openers.example: I was already halfway up the stairs with the tray when the lift doors finally opened behind me.
openers.why: Starts the reader inside a moment instead of walking them to it, which is the fastest route out of the flat 'It was a sunny day' opening.

openers.example: There were two hundred flyers, one afternoon and eleven blocks between me and dinner.
openers.why: Numbers create a deadline in the first sentence, and deadline pressure is the cheapest form of tension available.

openers.example: Clutching the torn letter, I ran the length of the corridor.
openers.why: Puts an action before the subject, so the sentence opens with movement instead of 'I'. Also fixes the habit of starting three sentences in a row with 'I'.

openers.example: Squinting against the glare off the badminton court, Malik missed the step entirely.
openers.why: Combines an opener with a small piece of plot. Check for the dangling participle: the -ing verb must belong to the subject of the main clause.

openers.template: Trying not to [do the obvious thing], [main clause].
openers.example: Trying not to look at the clock above the whiteboard, I read the same line four times.
openers.why: Shows anxiety through what the character resists doing, which is stronger than naming the anxiety.

openers.example: Exhausted by the third climb up to the fourteenth floor, I sat down on the kerb outside the lift lobby.
openers.why: Front-loads the cause of the character's state. Efficient at the start of a build-up paragraph.

openers.example: Cornered between the fence and the big drain, I had nowhere left to go.
openers.why: Physically boxes the character in before the reader knows why, which creates a question in sentence one.

openers.example: Reluctantly, I raised my hand.
openers.why: One word does the work of a whole clause of explanation. Avoid the tired defaults: Suddenly, Finally, Then, After that, Next.

openers.example: Ten minutes before the bell, the classroom door opened and it was not our teacher.
openers.why: Establishes a countdown. The reader now knows something must happen inside those ten minutes.

openers.example: For reasons I still cannot explain, I said yes.
openers.why: Creates immediate curiosity and gives the narrator a reflective voice, which is an AL1 marker.

openers.example: Beneath the void deck, three cats had claimed the bicycle rack for the afternoon.
openers.why: Sets the location with a specific inhabitant rather than a general description. Singapore detail costs nothing and reads as observed rather than invented.

openers.template: Under [light source], [the object looked different from how it looked before].
openers.example: Under the flickering corridor light, the note looked far worse than it had at home.
openers.why: Changes the meaning of an object by changing the light on it, which shows the character's shifting state without stating it.

openers.example: As the last bus pulled away from the interchange, I realised my wallet was still on the seat.
openers.why: Puts two events in the same sentence so the plot moves twice as fast in the opening.

openers.example: Although I had rehearsed it eleven times in the shower, my voice came out wrong on the first word.
openers.why: Sets up preparation and failure in one sentence, which is the shape of most good build-ups.

openers.example: Until that afternoon, I had thought of him as loud and nothing else.
openers.why: Announces that a judgement is about to be corrected, which is the engine of every empathy story.

openers.template: "[Line that raises a question]," [tag or action beat].
openers.example: "Don't tell anyone you saw me here," he said, and pulled his cap lower.
openers.why: Character, emotion and situation arrive at the same time. The strongest opener type for stories with two people in them.

openers.example: "You promised," she said, and that was the worst part.
openers.why: Opens on the conflict itself. Keep the narrator's reaction short so the line lands.

openers.template: [One precise sound or smell] [verb], and [what it told the character].
openers.example: The smell of burnt toast reached the corridor before I did, and I knew my father had tried again.
openers.why: Uses one sense rather than five. Three to four well-placed sensory details across a whole composition is the target; do not spend them all here.

openers.example: The ceiling fan clicked once. Then nothing. Then it clicked again, louder.
openers.why: Builds atmosphere with repetition and a gap. The absence of sound is more unsettling than any adjective.

openers.template: [Two to five words stating the fact].
openers.example: The lock had been changed.
openers.why: A very short opening sentence forces the second sentence to explain, which pulls the reader in. Use once, at the opening or at the climax, never both.

openers.template: [Question the narrator cannot yet answer], and [what they did instead].
openers.example: How do you tell your best friend that you were the one who told? I spent the whole of recess not answering that.
openers.why: Puts the story's moral problem in sentence one. Use at most one rhetorical question in the whole composition.

openers.template: [Pleasant weather detail], [but the character's situation contradicts it].
openers.example: It was the kind of clear morning the school photographer had prayed for, and I had spent it in the general office.
openers.why: Replaces the banned 'It was a sunny day' opening by making the weather do a job: contrast. Never describe weather without giving it a purpose.

openers.template: The rain [specific action it performed], and [the consequence for the character].
openers.example: The rain came down hard enough to bounce off the covered walkway, and the queue for the taxi stand stopped moving altogether.
openers.why: Shows weather through its effect on people rather than through adjectives about the sky.

openers.template: [Sentence containing the sound word inside it, not isolated].
openers.example: A single hollow clang came from somewhere inside the locker bay, and everybody in the corridor turned.
openers.why: Sound openings are heavily overused as isolated exclamations. Embedding the sound inside a sentence keeps the atmosphere and loses the cliche. Never open with Ring! Ring!, Chirp! Chirp! or Bang!

openers.example: The badminton racket is still behind the shoe cabinet, and I have not touched it since the day of the semi-final.
openers.why: Lets you open at the emotional end of the story and then explain how it got there. Handle the tense change carefully: present for the frame, past for the memory.

transitions.note: 'Worse still' and 'what was more' carry emotion as well as logic, so they suit narrative better than the essay-style 'moreover'.
'And yet' at the start of a sentence is a strong turn. 'The truth was' is the narrative version of 'however' and reads far less mechanical.
'Which was why' lets you attach the consequence to the same sentence, keeping the pace up. Save 'consequently' for Situational Writing; it is too formal for a narrative.
Ban 'Then', 'After that' and 'Next' as habitual paragraph openers. 'No sooner had' requires inversion: 'No sooner had I sat down than the bell rang.'

options: the whole of the next term
for the rest of the holidays
by the time the exams came
transitions.note: Anchor time shifts to the Singapore school calendar. Concrete markers such as 'by the September holidays' are more convincing than 'a long time later'.

options: on the corner of the page
transitions.note: A zoom-in transition moves the reader from the wide shot to the single detail. This is where your best sensory detail belongs.

options: back when we were in Primary Four
it had started long before that
this was not the first time
transitions.note: Move into a flashback with the past perfect ('it had started'), then settle into the simple past. Move out with a present-moment detail so the reader knows you have returned.
Transitions at the climax should be short. The long, long, short pattern works here: two long sentences to build, one short one to land.

options: by the time the lights came back on
transitions.note: 'What happened next was quieter' signals a deliberate drop in intensity, which is exactly what a falling-action paragraph is for.

options: it took me a term to understand
I have not told anyone that
transitions.note: Use at most one of these, in the final paragraph. Two reflective transitions in one composition makes the ending feel repeated.

endings.template: [Object from paragraph 1] is still [where it was], [but one thing about it has changed].
endings.example: The letter is still in my drawer, folded along the same crease. I have simply stopped reading it every night.
endings.why: Rewards the reader for remembering your opening, and shows change without stating it. The single most reliable AL1 ending.

endings.template: [Return to the opening location], [and describe what is different about it now].
endings.example: I walk past the bicycle rack every morning. The cats are still there. I am the one who stops now.

endings.template: [Time marker] I [small specific action that proves the change]. [Nobody noticed]. [That was the point].
endings.example: On Monday I got there ten minutes early and stacked the chairs before anyone asked. Nobody noticed. That was rather the point.
endings.why: Proves the value through behaviour instead of announcing it, which is the difference between the top band and the band below.

endings.template: I still [old habit], [but now I also do the new thing].
endings.example: I still take the lift to the fourteenth floor. I just knock on Mrs Kaur's door on the way past.
endings.why: Honest about partial change, which reads as more mature than a total transformation.

endings.template: [General observation about how the world works], [expressed as a fact, not a lesson].
endings.example: Courage, it turns out, is mostly a matter of who moves first.
endings.why: An indirect moral. It lands the value without the banned 'I learnt a valuable lesson' construction.

endings.template: [Emotion the reader expects], [denied]. [The truer, smaller emotion].
endings.example: I did not feel brave. I felt lighter, which is a different thing, and better.
endings.why: Undercutting the expected feeling makes the narrator sound honest, and honesty is what the top band rewards.

endings.template: I have not [done the difficult thing] yet. I will [do it], [at a specific time], [while the nerve lasts].
endings.example: I have not told my mother yet. I will tell her tonight, before dinner, while I still have the nerve.
endings.why: A decision that is specific and small enough to believe. Ends on forward motion rather than a summary.

endings.template: [Next scheduled event] is in [time]. [What the character intends to do differently].
endings.example: The next inter-class match is in March. I have already asked Coach if I can try the other position.

endings.template: "[Line from the other character]," [tag]. "[Narrator's short reply]," [and the action that carries the meaning].
endings.example: "You came back," Wei Ming said. "I did," I said, and picked up the other end of the box.
endings.why: Lets an action carry the emotion you have refused to state. Very strong for friendship and reconciliation stories.

endings.template: "[Question from another character]." [The narrator's answer is an action, not words].
endings.example: "Are we okay?" she asked. I moved my bag off the seat beside me.

endings.template: [One last precise sensory detail], [and the sense that ordinary life has resumed].
endings.example: The corridor smelt of floor polish and somebody's curry puff again, which meant the afternoon had gone back to being an ordinary one.
endings.why: Signals the end of tension through the senses rather than through explanation. Suits stories that ended in relief.

endings.template: [Sound of ordinary life returning], [and the character's small physical release].
endings.example: Downstairs, somebody started a scooter. My shoulders came down from somewhere near my ears.

endings.template: [The character still pays the price], [and accepts it], [with one surprising admission].
endings.example: I was taken off the relay team for the final. I still think I would do the same thing again, which surprises me more than it should.
endings.why: Refuses the easy happy ending. Costs nothing in marks and gains a great deal in maturity, provided the conflict is genuinely resolved.

endings.template: We are not [the ideal state] again. We are [the smaller true state], [and that is more than before].
endings.example: We are not friends again. We are two people who nod in the corridor, and last month we were not even that.
endings.why: Hope with a limit on it. Far more convincing than 'everything went back to normal'.

endings.template: [The character does not say the thing]. [Instead they do the small thing].
endings.example: I did not tell my grandmother that I had read the letter. I simply started making the coffee at six, the way she liked it.
endings.why: Gratitude proved rather than declared. Works especially well for family topics.

bannedPhrases.phrase: I learnt a valuable lesson that day
bannedPhrases.why: It announces the moral instead of showing it, and it is the single most common closing sentence in PSLE scripts. The marker has read it a dozen times that morning.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Close on a small concrete action that proves the change: 'On Monday I got there ten minutes early and stacked the chairs before anyone asked.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: And then I woke up. It was all a dream.
bannedPhrases.why: It cancels the entire plot, so the conflict the Content mark depends on turns out never to have happened.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Let the events be real and pay their consequences. If you need a strange event, make it a misunderstanding rather than a dream.

bannedPhrases.phrase: It was the best day of my life
bannedPhrases.why: A superlative with no evidence behind it. It tells the reader how to feel instead of earning the feeling.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Give the one detail you will remember: 'I still have the paper cup with the number 4 written on it in marker.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: It was a day I will never forget
bannedPhrases.why: Interchangeable with any other composition ever written. It adds no information at all.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Name what specifically will not be forgotten, and stop there.

bannedPhrases.phrase: It was a bright and sunny day
bannedPhrases.why: The most common opening in Singapore primary composition, and it does no work: the weather has nothing to do with the plot.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Open in the middle of an action, or give the weather a job through contrast: 'It was the kind of clear morning the school photographer had prayed for, and I had spent it in the general office.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: Ring! Ring! / Riiiing! / Chirp! Chirp!
bannedPhrases.why: Isolated sound-effect openings appear so often that they have lost all atmospheric effect, and the exclamation mark makes it worse.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Embed the sound in a sentence and make it specific to your story: 'A single hollow clang came from somewhere inside the locker bay.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: Suddenly, ...
bannedPhrases.why: Used as a habitual opener it stops meaning anything, and it often signals an event the writer did not prepare for.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Use 'That was when' or simply start the sentence with the event itself. If the event is genuinely sudden, a short sentence delivers it better than the word 'suddenly'.

bannedPhrases.phrase: a wave of [emotion] washed over me
bannedPhrases.why: Overused for every emotion in P5 and P6 scripts, and it describes the emotion as weather happening to the character instead of something they experience.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Show the body: 'My hands went still on the desk and stayed there.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: my heart sank / my heart leapt
bannedPhrases.why: Acceptable once in a composition; most students use one of them three times, at which point it is invisible.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Vary the location: 'The bottom dropped out of my stomach', or use a thought instead of a body part.

bannedPhrases.phrase: words cannot describe how I felt
bannedPhrases.why: It is an admission that you have not attempted the task, and description is exactly what the Language mark is for.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Attempt the description. One honest ordinary detail beats an apology: 'I read the message three times, then read it again in case it changed.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: Last but not least
bannedPhrases.why: Belongs in a speech or a list, not in a narrative. It signals memorised structure.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Use a narrative sequence transition such as 'By the time the last bus left' or simply start the paragraph with the action.

bannedPhrases.phrase: In conclusion, ...
bannedPhrases.why: This is essay language. In a story it tells the marker you have run out of narrative and switched into an answer format.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: End on an image, an action or a short honest sentence. Stories do not need signposting.

bannedPhrases.phrase: I was very happy / very sad / very scared
bannedPhrases.why: 'Very' plus a basic emotion word is the clearest signal of the middle bands. It names a feeling instead of creating it.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Pick two of body, thought and sense: 'My cheeks ached before I noticed I had been smiling.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: we all lived happily ever after
bannedPhrases.why: A fairy-tale close on a realistic narrative, and it resolves nothing specific.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Resolve the actual conflict from paragraph four, then show one changed detail.

bannedPhrases.phrase: everyone praised me and I felt so proud of myself
bannedPhrases.why: A self-congratulatory close. It shifts the ending from character change to applause, which markers read as a weaker resolution.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: 'I did not need to tell anyone. That was new.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: From that day on, I promised myself I would never do it again
bannedPhrases.why: A vow this large is not believable from a twelve-year-old and reads as a formula.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Make the promise small, specific and slightly doubted: 'I have not touched his things since. It has been eleven days, which is not very long, but it is a start.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: Fortunately, my teacher arrived just in time
bannedPhrases.why: An adult rescue removes the character's agency, and the Content mark depends on the main character resolving the conflict.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: Let the character act, even imperfectly, and let the adult arrive afterwards to deal with the consequences.

bannedPhrases.phrase: All's well that ends well
bannedPhrases.why: A proverb as a final sentence does the reflection's job badly and reads as memorised.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: An indirect observation instead: 'We did not agree. We simply stopped needing to.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: I quickly ran as fast as I could
bannedPhrases.why: Three words doing one word's job, and 'quickly' plus 'as fast as I could' is redundant.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: One strong verb plus a landmark: 'I tore past the bicycle bays and did not slow down until the lift lobby.'

bannedPhrases.phrase: little did I know what was about to happen
bannedPhrases.why: It tells the marker a twist is coming, so the twist is no longer a twist.
bannedPhrases.insteadTry: End the paragraph on an ordinary detail. Let the surprise arrive without a warning label.

showNotTell.showing: My fingers would not close around the door handle. I told them to, twice.
I counted the footsteps behind me and lost count at four, which was worse than counting.
My feet had made a different plan from the rest of me and were not consulting anybody.
I gripped the corridor railing until my knuckles went pale, mostly so my hands would stop.
The ceiling fan clicked. Then nothing. Then it clicked again, louder.
The paper shook, so I put it flat on the table and pretended I had meant to all along.

showNotTell.telling: I was worried about the results.
showNotTell.showing: I had checked my bag for the slip four times, and it was in the same pocket each time.

showNotTell.telling: I was too nervous to eat.
showNotTell.showing: I picked the beansprouts out of the noodles one at a time and lined them up on the edge of the plate.
I read the same line four times and could not have told you a single word of it.
I read the message three times, then read it again in case it had changed.
I laughed at nothing at all, in an empty corridor, on my own.
My schoolbag hit the floor before I had decided to drop it.
My cheeks ached before I noticed I had been smiling.
I had packed the bag twice and unpacked it once, just so I could pack it again.
I put the cup down very, very carefully, because the alternative was throwing it.
The words were already out of my mouth, sharpened, before I had chosen them.
My voice arrived in the classroom before I did.
I could hear my own breathing, which is never a good sign.
There were four small crescents in my palm afterwards, and I did not remember making them.
I ate dinner because it was in front of me, not because I wanted any of it.
I turned the tap on first, so that nobody in the corridor would hear.
I sat at our usual table in the canteen. It only needed one chair now.
Her handwriting was still on the shopping list stuck to the fridge, and I still had not taken it down.
The flat made exactly the same sounds it always had. That was the problem.
I could not look at the space above his eyebrows, let alone at his eyes.

showNotTell.telling: I was ashamed of what I had done.
showNotTell.showing: "Nothing," I said, when my mother asked what had happened at school, and I hated how easily it came out.
I studied the grout between two floor tiles as though it were going to be tested.

showNotTell.telling: I did not deserve the prize.
showNotTell.showing: I put the trophy at the back of the shelf, behind my father's dictionary.
I had told the truth about everything except the one part that mattered.
I rehearsed the apology in the shower for four days and delivered none of them.
The fifty-dollar note stayed in my pocket all afternoon, and it got heavier every hour.

showNotTell.telling: I knew I was wrong to join in.
showNotTell.showing: I laughed with the others. I laughed one full second later than the others.
I did not need to tell anybody. That was new.
I folded the certificate along the crease my father had made, and kept it in the back of my file.

showNotTell.telling: I was proud of my sister.
showNotTell.showing: I clapped until the man beside me turned to look, and then I clapped anyway.
The time on the screen started with a 2 for the first time. I read it twice to be sure.

showNotTell.telling: I heaved a sigh of relief.
showNotTell.showing: My shoulders came down from somewhere near my ears.
I realised I had been holding my bag with both hands the entire time.
The corridor had a smell again: floor polish, and somebody's curry puff.
He was complaining about the bandage. Complaining meant he was fine.
I heard my own name inside somebody else's laugh.
My ears were hot, which meant everyone behind me could see it too.

showNotTell.telling: I wished the ground would swallow me.
showNotTell.showing: I bent down to tie a shoelace that was already tied.
Thirty-one people found it funny. I counted, because I had nothing else to do with the next minute.
I set the alarm for half past five and moved the phone across the room so I would have to stand up.
I taped the failed attempt above my desk, where I would have to look at it every evening.
My palms were raw. I chalked them and got back on the bar.
The finish line had not moved. I put one foot in front of the other and stopped negotiating with myself.

showNotTell.telling: I had no friends in the new class.
showNotTell.showing: I learnt the route to the toilet that took longest, and used it at every recess.
I had two conversations that whole week and one of them was with the drinks stall auntie.

showNotTell.telling: I was grateful to my mother.
showNotTell.showing: The receipt in her purse was dated three months before mine, and she had never once mentioned it.
"Thank you, Ah Ma," I said, using her name for the first time in years, and she pretended not to notice.
I congratulated him with the right words, in the right order, at the wrong volume.
I turned my paper over before she got to my desk, and told myself it was because the fan was blowing it.
I took the stairs one at a time, both feet on each step, like my grandfather does.
I sat down on the kerb outside the lift lobby without checking whether it was clean.
I said "what" out loud, to nobody, in an empty stairwell.
I checked the name on the list again, then checked the year, then checked the name again.
I put the training shoes by the door on Sunday night, which I had not done since March.

showNotTell.telling: I wished I had never said it.
showNotTell.showing: I typed the message, deleted it, and typed a shorter one that was somehow worse.

structures.name: Story Mountain
stages: Beginning: character, setting, and a tension already running
Unexpected event: the thing that creates the main problem
Build-up: complications that raise the stakes
Climax: the single most intense moment, written as one complete scene
Falling action: the consequence of the climax
Ending: the character's change, shown
structures.howToUse: Sketch six boxes on the rough paper before writing. Write two or three words in each. If two boxes contain the same idea, your plot is thin and you should replace one of them. Spend the most words on the climax box.
structures.worksBestFor: Any PSLE narrative. This is the default plan and the one to use if you have less than five minutes to plan.

structures.name: FAST (climax paragraph)
stages: Feeling: what the body is doing, not the emotion word
Action: what the character physically does
Speech: one line of dialogue, or one line deliberately not said
Thought: the single sentence running through the character's head
structures.howToUse: Apply only to the climax paragraph. Include all four elements in that paragraph, in any order, and keep the sentences shorter than in the rest of the composition. Do not place an idiom here.
structures.worksBestFor: Turning the most important eighty to a hundred and ten words into a scene instead of a summary.

structures.name: MFHD (ending)
stages: Moral: an indirect observation about the world
Feeling: one honest, unembellished emotion
Hope: a hope with a limit on it
Decision: a small, specific, believable next step
structures.howToUse: Choose one or two of the four. Never use all four, which produces a bloated four-sentence moral. The strongest pairings are Feeling plus Decision, and Moral plus Hope.
structures.worksBestFor: Ending in three to six sentences without writing 'I learnt a valuable lesson'.

structures.name: 5W1H planning
stages: Who is in the story and who changes
Where it happens, precisely
When it happens, including the time pressure
What the problem is
Why the problem matters to this character
How it is resolved by the character's own action
structures.howToUse: Answer all six in single words before you write. The 'Why' answer is the one that produces Content marks, because it is what makes the conflict matter.
structures.worksBestFor: Topics where you have an idea but no plot yet, and for checking that your ending is not a coincidence.

structures.name: Three Openings drill
stages: Write an action opening for the topic
Write a dialogue opening for the same topic
Write a sensory opening for the same topic
Compare and keep the one that raises the most questions
structures.howToUse: Spend three minutes and roughly twenty-five words on each. The one you keep is usually not the first one you wrote. This is a practice drill, not an exam-day activity.
structures.worksBestFor: Breaking the habit of always opening the same way, and for building a bank of openings you can adapt under exam conditions.

structures.name: Long, long, short
stages: Long sentence that builds the situation
Long sentence that adds the complication
Short sentence, two to five words, that lands the moment
structures.howToUse: Use once at the climax and, if you like, once at the very end of the composition. Using it in every paragraph destroys the effect, because the short sentence only works against long ones.
structures.worksBestFor: The Language mark, which rewards sentence variety used for effect rather than variety for its own sake.

structures.name: Five-part PSLE plan
stages: Opening: who, where, when
Build-up: what triggers the main event
Climax: the most intense moment
Resolution: how it is settled
Ending: what the character feels or has become
structures.howToUse: A compressed version of the Story Mountain for when the topic is simple. Assign a rough word budget to each: 60, 90, 100, 60, 50.
structures.worksBestFor: Reflective or relationship topics where there is no dramatic external event.

structures.name: Value-woven plan
stages: Choose the CCE value the topic points at
Show the character lacking it in paragraph one or two
Make the climax a moment where the value is costly
Have the character choose the value and pay the cost
End with a small action that proves the change, never a statement
structures.howToUse: Use this on top of the Story Mountain, not instead of it. The check is simple: if the reader could name the value without the last paragraph, you have woven it correctly.
structures.worksBestFor: The very common PSLE topics of honesty, kindness, responsibility, perseverance and forgiveness.

structures.name: Deadline device
stages: Name a fixed time or limit early: a bell, a closing gate, a departing bus, a hospital visiting hour
Refer to it once in the build-up
Refer to it again just before the climax
Let it run out or be met at the climax
structures.howToUse: Suspense comes from how a story is told, not what happens in it. A deadline makes small actions feel urgent, so an ordinary story about returning a wallet can hold tension.
structures.worksBestFor: Topics with low natural drama, where you need tension without inventing an accident or a crime.

dialogueCraft.example:
"You took it," she said.
"I borrowed it," I said, which was not true and we both knew it.
dialogueCraft.why: Punctuation and paragraphing sit inside the Language mark. Running two speakers together in one paragraph confuses the reader and costs marks even when the words are good.

dialogueCraft.move: Comma inside the closing quotation mark before a tag
dialogueCraft.why: The full stop only appears inside the quotation mark when no tag follows: "I'm ready." He picked up his bag. Getting this wrong is one of the most common punctuation errors in P6 scripts.

dialogueCraft.move: No capital letter after a mid-sentence tag
dialogueCraft.why: The sentence continues, so 'you' stays lower case. If the tag ends the sentence, the next quotation starts with a capital: "Wait," he said. "You dropped this."

dialogueCraft.move: Action beat instead of an adverb
dialogueCraft.example: "It's fine." She stacked the plates without looking up.
dialogueCraft.why: Replaces 'she said coldly' with evidence. Adverbs on speech tags are the fastest way to tell instead of show.

dialogueCraft.example: "You went anyway." It was not a question.
dialogueCraft.why: A tag-free line that comments on the speech. This is an AL1 move because it shows the narrator interpreting, not just reporting.

dialogueCraft.example: "I'm fine," she said. She was not fine.
dialogueCraft.why: Two short sentences create a gap between what is said and what is true, which is where all narrative tension lives.

dialogueCraft.example:
"But I only wanted to—"
"You wanted to win," he said.
dialogueCraft.why: The dash inside the quotation marks shows the sentence being cut off. Correct punctuation of interruption is rare in P6 scripts and stands out to a marker.

dialogueCraft.example: "I only meant..." I could not find the end of the sentence.
dialogueCraft.why: Three dots show a thought that runs out, which suits confession and embarrassment scenes. Use once; more than that looks like uncertainty about punctuation.

dialogueCraft.example: "Sit down," Mr Tan said. "Both of you."
dialogueCraft.why: Readers do not notice 'said', which lets your one or two loaded verbs land hard. A page where every tag is 'exclaimed', 'retorted' and 'bellowed' reads as strained.

dialogueCraft.move: One loaded speech verb, well placed
dialogueCraft.example: "It was me," I admitted, and the classroom went very quiet.
dialogueCraft.why: 'Admitted' does the work of a whole sentence of explanation. Save these verbs for the two or three lines that carry the plot.

dialogueCraft.move: Dialogue that carries plot, not chat
dialogueCraft.example: "Your name is on the sign-out sheet," she said.
dialogueCraft.why: Every line of speech should either move the plot or reveal character. Greetings and small talk waste words you need for the climax.

dialogueCraft.example: "Later I help you carry, okay?" my grandmother said.
dialogueCraft.why: Natural rhythm is fine and often reads as authentic. Avoid heavy phonetic spelling, which markers read as informal register rather than characterisation.

dialogueCraft.example: "Are you going to tell her?" I asked. He picked up his bag and left the void deck.
dialogueCraft.why: Refusing to answer is stronger than any line of dialogue, and it forces the reader to interpret.

climaxTechniques.name: Slow the clock
climaxTechniques.how: Break one moment into three or four separate actions, each in its own short sentence. Time in a story is measured in sentences, not in minutes.
climaxTechniques.example: The rope moved. My hand slipped to the second knot. Somebody below me said my name. I did not look down.

climaxTechniques.name: Full FAST scene
climaxTechniques.how: Include Feeling, Action, Speech and Thought inside the climax paragraph. Any one lifts the paragraph; all four make it a scene rather than a summary.
climaxTechniques.example: My hands would not stay still on the railing. I climbed the last two steps anyway. "I'm coming," I called, and hoped somebody was listening. If she had gone in already, I was too late.

climaxTechniques.name: Sensory density spike
climaxTechniques.how: Place your best two sensory details here, at the point of highest tension, rather than spreading four thin details evenly across the composition.
climaxTechniques.example: The stairwell smelt of wet cement and drain water. Somewhere above me a metal door banged twice and then stayed shut.

climaxTechniques.name: The short sentence landing
climaxTechniques.how: Two long sentences build the moment; one sentence of two to five words lands it. The short one must contain the fact, not a feeling.
climaxTechniques.example: I had rehearsed what I would say the whole way up in the lift, and I had a version for every possible face she might make when she opened the door. I knocked, and the sound was much smaller than I expected. Nobody came.

climaxTechniques.name: Sound then silence
climaxTechniques.how: Give one sharp sound, then remove all sound. The gap does more work than any adjective about tension.
climaxTechniques.example: The gate rattled once. After that the whole corridor was so still that I could hear the lift cables moving two floors down.

climaxTechniques.name: Deadline runs out
climaxTechniques.how: Refer to the time limit you established earlier, at the exact moment it expires. This converts an ordinary event into a crisis without adding any new plot.
climaxTechniques.example: The security guard reached up and pulled the first shutter down. Visiting hours had four minutes left in them and I was still on the wrong side of the road.

climaxTechniques.name: Dilemma stated in one line
climaxTechniques.how: Put the impossible choice into a single sentence of internal thought. Inner conflict earns Content marks because it shows the character has something at stake.
climaxTechniques.example: I could tell the truth and lose the team, or say nothing and lose the only thing I actually liked about myself.

climaxTechniques.name: The refused rescue
climaxTechniques.how: Have help nearly arrive, then not arrive, so the character must act alone. This protects your Content mark from the coincidence problem.
climaxTechniques.example: Mrs Devi's classroom light was still on. I was three steps from her door when it went off and the corridor went dark, and it was still my problem.

climaxTechniques.name: One fresh simile only
climaxTechniques.how: The climax is the single place a simile is worth spending, and it must not be from any memorised list. Compare to something ordinary and specific.
climaxTechniques.example: The hall had gone as quiet as a lift between floors.

climaxTechniques.name: No idioms at the peak
climaxTechniques.how: Idioms compress meaning, and compression is the opposite of what the climax needs. Write the moment out in your own concrete words instead.
climaxTechniques.example: Not: 'My heart was in my mouth.' Instead: 'I was breathing through my mouth because my nose had stopped being enough.'

climaxTechniques.name: The physical consequence
climaxTechniques.how: Let the climax leave a mark on the character's body or on an object. A consequence the reader can see makes the resolution feel earned.
climaxTechniques.example: The strap left a red line across my palm that was still there at dinner, and my mother did not ask about it.
